fatal_errors: The proposed Cu-coated-graphene addition does not reconstruct the target intervention: liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu.
The hypothesis omits selective Ti-rich interdendrite dissolution, retention of RHEA ligaments, and formation of the approximately 300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer central to the target mechanism.

Claims concerning irradiation-induced void suppression and neutron/ion service performance are not supported by the cited evidence, which reports processing, conductivity, hardness, and suppression of WC formation rather than irradiation testing.
The starting material, processing duration, resulting phase fractions, directional architecture, and temperature-dependent thermal crossover relative to pure W are inconsistent with the target.
explanation: This is a coherent, testable alternative based on published Cu@Gr-doped W–Cu processing rather than a reconstruction of the hidden study. The cited paper directly supports 0.8 wt.% Cu@Gr, SPS at 1280 °C and 30 MPa for 10 minutes, and a 24.3% thermal-conductivity increase, so the comparative thermal claim has a legitimate basis. The paired-control experiment is reasonably discriminating, although irradiation type, dose, temperature, and quantitative damage metrics are underspecified. Evidence does not substantiate the proposed capillary-wetting, Cu-evaporation prevention, interfacial-void suppression under irradiation, or neutron-service claims. The target instead used 1200 °C/96 h liquid-metal dealloying of WTaVTi to generate aligned RHEA and nearly pure Cu networks, with a W-rich interlayer, a roughly 4.4-fold room-temperature conductivity increase over the precursor, high-temperature crossover above pure W, and only proxy He-ion testing of precursor dendrites.
